questions.question: While reviewing trend logs for an air-handling unit controller, an electrician notices the supply-air temperature trace diverges from the commissioned setpoint curve after a recent firmware update. An alarm was acknowledged, but no cause was logged. What action maintains proper control of the situation?
options: Adjust several loop tuning parameters at once and treat any temporary stabilization as proof the issue is fixed.
Apply the trend baseline from a similar AHU in another building without verifying this unit's actual sequence.
Pause, compare the trend data to the approved sequence of operations, resolve the discrepancy, and document findings before proceeding.
Replace the sensor with the greatest calibration drift first and document the cause only if the fault returns.
questions.explanation: An undocumented alarm and a trend that no longer matches the commissioned setpoint curve signal an unverified control discrepancy, not a confirmed hardware fault. The correct response is to stop, compare live trend data against the approved sequence of operations and commissioning records, identify the actual cause, and log the resolution before continuing—this preserves an auditable, verifiable change history. Adjusting multiple parameters simultaneously masks the true cause and makes any apparent improvement unreliable. Borrowing a baseline from a different unit ignores this AHU's specific sequence and equipment configuration, risking incorrect commands. Replacing hardware before confirming the cause wastes resources and may leave the real fault unresolved, since the discrepancy could stem from firmware logic changes rather than sensor drift.

questions.question: An air handling unit has run in manual override for several months after a nuisance freezestat alarm. A tenant fit-up now requires the automatic sequence to resume. Before removing the override on unit E28-09, what should the electrician confirm first?
options: Return the unit to automatic and watch discharge air temperature through one full occupied cycle before checking anything else.
Confirm override status against the approved control drawings, equipment ratings, manufacturer data, and current field readings.
Match the occupied and unoccupied setpoints on the building automation graphic to the tenant's new schedule and save the change.
Have the building operator describe the original nuisance alarm and enter that description as the record of the override's cause.
questions.explanation: An extended override can mask a real fault, so returning to automatic control without verification risks unstable operation, incorrect commands, or loss of protective action such as freeze protection. Comparing the override status against approved control drawings, rated equipment parameters, manufacturer data, and measured field values confirms whether the original cause is resolved before automatic sequencing is restored. Releasing the unit to automatic and observing one cycle tests the system with an unverified fault still possible and no baseline to interpret what is seen. Adjusting occupied and unoccupied setpoints addresses the tenant schedule but does nothing to prove the overridden point, sensor, or interlock now functions as designed. An operator's spoken account of the alarm is useful background, but it is not measured evidence and cannot confirm current device condition or wiring integrity. Only the verified, documented comparison supports a traceable decision that the next shift can independently confirm.

questions.question: Trend logs on a rooftop AHU show its heating/cooling sequence intermittently skips a stage every third cycle, but only during shoulder-season mornings. Occupants report brief temperature swings. Which response gives the most reliable resolution?
options: Rely on the building operator's recollection of past behaviour as the acceptance record for the sequence.
Complete remaining programming and treat the next full energization as the first check of the sequence.
Isolate the affected control loop, test the sequence logic, fix the confirmed cause, then repeat a controlled functional test.
Accept the sequence as correct because an identical AHU performed properly on a prior job site.
questions.explanation: An intermittent staging fault tied to a specific temperature window points to a real but occasional condition-such as a sensor drift, timer race, or point-mapping error-that only a controlled, isolated test can confirm and fix. Isolating the loop lets the technician force conditions matching the reported pattern, verify the corrected logic against the points list and sequence description, and repeat the functional test to prove the fix holds before returning it to normal service. Relying on memory or a colleague's past success ignores this unit's actual trend data. Treating energization as the first test risks repeating the fault live during occupied hours, and assuming correctness from a similar prior installation overlooks documented evidence that this specific sequence is behaving incorrectly. Only a targeted, repeatable verification against recorded evidence and approved commissioning documentation reliably closes out an intermittent fault.

questions.question: A rooftop unit's discharge air control follows the closed loop shown in the diagram: sensor measurement feeds the controller, the controller drives the actuator, the process responds, and the result is fed back to the controller. During commissioning, the electrician finds the discharge air transmitter configured for 0-50°C while the approved points list specifies 0-100°C, and the modulating valve is hunting. Because the error enters the loop at the sensor measurement block, every controller decision is made on a feedback value that is roughly double the actual temperature. What is the correct next action?
options: Widen the controller's proportional band and lengthen the integral time until the actuator output settles, leaving the transmitter configured for 0-50°C.
Leave the transmitter range as found and enter a fixed offset at the controller input so the displayed discharge temperature matches a handheld thermometer at the present operating temperature.
Replace the discharge air transmitter with a wider-range unit and re-verify actuator stroke, on the assumption the hunting is caused by a failing sensor element.

Take the loop out of automatic control, reset the transmitter range to the specified 0-100°C, confirm the controller input scaling matches, then check that feedback tracks actual temperature and record the change.
questions.explanation: In the loop shown, the controller can only act on the number arriving from the sensor measurement block. A 0-50°C transmitter feeding a controller expecting 0-100°C sends a signal that overstates temperature across the whole range, so the controller over-drives the valve, the process overshoots, and the feedback path sustains the hunting. Correcting the range at its source, confirming the controller's input scaling agrees, then watching feedback follow real temperature restores an accurate loop and leaves a record of what was changed. Retuning the proportional band and integral time only slows the actuator's reaction to a false measurement, so the discharge temperature still stabilizes at the wrong value. A fixed offset cannot fix a span error, because a wrong span is off by a percentage of reading and only matches the reference at the single point where it was trimmed, drifting again as temperature changes. Replacing the transmitter spends time and material on hardware that is functioning correctly and simply configured for the wrong range, and the new unit will behave the same way if it is set up from the incorrect range.

questions.question: Tenants served by air handler AHU-6 report overheating. At the controller the electrician sees discharge-air temperature holding steady at 18 °C, the chilled-water valve almost fully closed, and the active discharge-air setpoint displaying 18 °C where the occupied cooling target should be 13 °C. Which response correctly addresses this control condition?
options: Enter a negative calibration offset on the discharge-air sensor so the controller reads colder than actual air and opens the chilled-water valve further.
Narrow the throttling range on the cooling loop so a small temperature error drives the chilled-water valve toward full open much sooner.

Trace what is writing the elevated value — a supply-air reset routine, an unoccupied or warm-up mode, or a retained local override — restore the 13 °C target, then confirm the valve modulates to hold it.
Command the chilled-water valve to a fixed 60 percent open for the remainder of the occupied period so supply air cools while the setpoint stays at 18 °C.
questions.explanation: Read the evidence first: measured temperature equals the active setpoint and the valve has backed nearly closed, which means the sensor, valve, and control loop are all working — they are simply driving toward the wrong target. A loop can only be as correct as the number written to its setpoint, so the troubleshooting effort belongs at the setpoint source. Common sources of an elevated value are a supply-air reset routine that raises the target as outdoor or return-air temperature falls, a mode-based setpoint left active from warm-up or unoccupied operation, and an override written at a higher command priority that was never released. Restoring 13 °C and then watching the valve stroke open and the discharge temperature pull down proves the loop responds. A negative sensor offset corrupts the feedback signal every alarm, trend, and reset calculation depends on, and it hides the real supply temperature from anyone who looks later. Narrowing the throttling range raises loop gain, which causes valve hunting and temperature swings, and it cannot lower a target the controller is already satisfying. Fixing the valve at 60 percent abandons closed-loop control altogether, so discharge temperature drifts with load and flow, risking overcooling, coil freeze conditions, and wasted terminal reheat while the wrong setpoint remains in place.

questions.question: During an economizer functional test on a rooftop unit, the outdoor air damper actuator drives fully closed each time the BAS commands 100% open, and the space temperature climbs steadily. Before this point is released back to automatic control, what should the electrician confirm?
options: That the 24 V supply and transformer capacity measured at the actuator terminals match the actuator's inrush and holding load
That the actuator's rotation/direction selection and control signal wiring produce opening travel on an increasing command, as shown in the sequence of operation
That the mixed air and outdoor air sensors read within tolerance of a calibrated reference thermometer at the damper inlet
That the BAS analog output has been rescaled so the software command matches the damper position now being reported
questions.explanation: A modulating damper actuator has a direction (CW/CCW) selection and a defined signal-to-travel relationship, plus a spring-return direction on loss of power. If the actuator strokes closed on an increasing open command, the direction selection or the control signal wiring is opposite to the documented sequence of operation, so the damper also fails in the wrong direction on power loss. Confirming the direction setting and signal wiring against the sequence of operation, then re-stroking the damper from 0% to 100%, proves the point behaves correctly before it runs unattended. Checking supply voltage and transformer capacity is worthwhile for actuators that stall or chatter, but a unit that strokes smoothly the wrong way is being powered adequately. Sensor calibration affects when the economizer is enabled and how far it modulates, not which way the actuator travels for a given command. Rescaling the analog output to make the software agree with observed position hides the reversal in the front end while the spring-return direction and any hardwired override still act backwards.

questions.question: During business hours, VAV zone controller E28-14 repeatedly drops to its unoccupied setpoints, but only while the 30 kW supply fan drive in the adjacent mechanical room ramps up to high speed. The controller is programmed to fall back to unoccupied defaults whenever it stops receiving the global occupied schedule broadcast from the front end over the BAS communication trunk. What is the most reliable next step?
options: Raise the unoccupied heating and cooling setpoints at the controller so the zone stays comfortable each time the fallback occurs.
Program the front end for a 24-hour occupied schedule so the zone is never issued an unoccupied command during the heating season.

Trend the controller's communication status while the drive ramps up to confirm whether the schedule broadcast is being lost, then correct the cable routing, shield termination, or bonding deficiency and retest under the same load.
Replace the zone temperature sensor and damper actuator on the affected box, then have occupants report whether the comfort complaints continue.
questions.explanation: The fallback to unoccupied setpoints is a programmed response to losing the occupied schedule broadcast, and the symptom appears only when a large drive is running, which points to induced noise on the communication trunk. Trending the communication status while the drive ramps confirms whether packets are actually being lost, so the cabling, shield termination, or bonding problem can be corrected and then proven by repeating the same load condition. Raising the unoccupied setpoints only hides the dropout while the controller still loses its schedule, so control remains unreliable. Forcing a 24-hour occupied schedule wastes fan and heating energy and still leaves the trunk vulnerable to interference that can affect other controllers. Changing the sensor and actuator addresses hardware that is not causing the mode change, since the zone follows its setpoints correctly once the schedule broadcast is received.

questions.question: On a rooftop air-handling unit, the supply-air high-temperature switch is wired to controller input 4, but in the controller database that input is addressed to the software point named "Exhaust Fan Status." The approved points list assigns input 4 to "Supply Air High Temp." As a result, when the switch closes the workstation annunciates an exhaust fan event and the high-temperature alarm never appears. What should the electrician do next?
options: Edit the workstation graphic text so the incoming alarm reads as a supply-air high-temperature event, leaving the input's point address as found.
Re-terminate the high-temperature switch conductors onto the input already addressed as exhaust fan status so the field wiring agrees with the existing database.
Create an additional software point for supply-air high temperature and leave the original address active as a second annunciation path.
Re-address input 4 to the supply-air high-temperature point named on the approved points list, retest by tripping the switch, and record the corrected mapping.
questions.explanation: Alarm mapping is only correct when the physical input, the software point address, and the approved points list all agree. Re-addressing input 4 to the supply-air high-temperature point, then tripping the switch to confirm the right alarm text and priority appear at the workstation, proves the signal path end to end; recording the corrected mapping keeps the as-built documentation usable by the next technician. Editing only the graphic text hides the fault: the underlying address still belongs to the exhaust fan point, so any interlock, alarm priority, or trend tied to that point continues to behave incorrectly. Re-terminating the switch to the exhaust-fan-addressed input makes the wiring match a database entry that itself contradicts the approved points list, and it leaves input 4 unused and unmonitored. Adding a duplicate point produces two annunciations from one contact, which inflates alarm counts and still leaves an unresolved conflict between the drawings and the installed configuration.
